query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tuning the propellant gas mixture in the HVAF-i7 torch to increase particle velocity will enhance impact momentum and splat formation, thus enabling a thicker, more adherent FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat with minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with particle size 15–45 μm prepared for HVAF-i7 deposition.
generation.intervention: Adjust the fuel-to-oxygen ratio in the HVAF-i7 torch to generate a higher in-flight particle velocity during deposition.
generation.conditions: Deposition conducted with the HVAF-i7 system on substrates including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm, under standard ambient conditions and within the established processing window for FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced in-flight particle kinetic energy resulting in improved splat deformation and consolidation on impact.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the fuel-to-oxygen ratio leads to a higher particle velocity, which improves momentum transfer on impact. This results in more effective splat flattening, minimized particle rebound, and reduced in-flight oxidation due to shorter dwell times at elevated temperatures. The enhanced bonding between deposited layers cumulatively produces a thicker coating without compromising adhesion or oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified process is expected to produce a significantly thicker, multi-layer bond coat with high adhesion and low oxidation levels relative to the baseline deposition using the 15–45 μm feedstock with standard propellant conditions.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with the standard HVAF-i7 parameters using 15–45 μm feedstock yield acceptable quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain effective within the typical HVAF-i7 operating conditions and when depositing on substrates featuring complex geometries (e.g., internal diameters around 120 mm). Its effectiveness may be limited outside the tested fuel-to-oxygen ratios or if excessive oxidation is induced by overly energetic particles.
generation.uncertainty: While increased particle velocity is predicted to improve deposition efficiency and coating thickness, there is uncertainty regarding the optimal balance between kinetic energy and in-flight oxidation risk. Detailed parameter optimization and further experimental validation are needed to define precise process windows.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled comparative study using the HVAF-i7 deposition process. One set of experiments will use the standard fuel-to-oxygen ratio (control group), while the experimental group will use an elevated fuel-to-oxygen ratio aimed at increasing particle velocity. All other deposition parameters (e.g., feedstock particle size, stand-off distance, substrate configuration) will be held constant.
measurements: In-flight particle velocity (using suitable diagnostic tools such as high-speed imaging or laser Doppler velocimetry)
Coating microstructure and splat formation (using SEM)
Oxide content and oxidation levels (using EDS and XRD analyses)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated propellant gas mixture does not yield a statistically significant (e.g., >20% improvement) increase in coating thickness and/or results in unacceptable increases in oxidation or diminished adhesion compared to the control, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. proposals.material_system: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy (HEA) powder with particle size 15–45 μm
proposals.intervention: Optimize the spray stand‐off distance for the HVAF-i7 torch to 300–350 mm
proposals.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch with the current feedstock on substrates (including internal diameters as small as 120 mm) at ambient to moderately heated substrate conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Improved in-flight particle momentum and impact splat formation
proposals.mechanism: A longer, optimized spray distance leads to particles acquiring a higher velocity and more favorable thermal histories, analogous to the improved deposition efficiency seen in conventional MCrAlY systems. The increased kinetic energy upon impact enhances splat flattening and inter-particle bonding, thereby building a thicker, adherent coating while limiting oxidation through controlled cooling.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A significantly thicker and highly adherent bond coat with minimal as-sprayed oxidation and maintained durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service compared to the baseline of inadequate thickness at shorter nozzle distances.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By replicating nozzle-specific spray distances shown to improve deposition efficiency in MCrAlY coatings, this intervention directly targets the thickness limitation observed with the HVAF-i7 system.

proposals.intervention: Enhance particle velocity by tuning the propellant gas mixture in the HVAF-i7 torch (e.g., adjusting fuel-to-oxygen ratio)
proposals.conditions: HVAF-i7 spraying under modified gas conditions with controlled ambient humidity and substrate preconditioning, ensuring deposition in confined internal diameters (≈120 mm)
proposals.structural_mediator: Higher in-flight particle kinetic energy and better splat formation
proposals.mechanism: Increasing the particle velocity improves momentum transfer upon impact, resulting in more efficient flattening and consolidation of particles. This facilitates a higher build-up rate while minimizing oxidation due to shorter dwell times at high temperatures.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A thicker and more robust HEA bond coating relative to the standard HVAF-i7 process, while maintaining acceptable oxidation levels and adhesion for high-temperature performance.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly addresses the coating thickness issue by increasing deposition efficiency through a different lever—process gas tuning—to boost particle velocity.

proposals.material_system: FeCoNiCrAl HEA powder (15–45 μm) deposited by HVAF-i7
proposals.intervention: Pre-heat the substrate prior to deposition
proposals.conditions: Substrate pre-heated to an optimized temperature (e.g., 200–300 °C) during HVAF-i7 spraying inside components with internal diameters down to 120 mm
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced splat wetting and inter-splat coalescence
proposals.mechanism: Pre-heating the substrate increases its surface energy and reduces thermal gradients at the coating–substrate interface, promoting better flattening, bonding, and overall deposition efficiency. This reduces stress and potential oxidation during rapid cooling, resulting in a thicker, more uniform bond coat.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A more uniformly thick and adherent bond coating with improved microstructural integrity and controlled oxidation compared to coatings deposited on room-temperature substrates.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By promoting better splat adhesion and reduced interfacial stresses, pre-heating supports layer build-up, directly countering the thickness limitation seen with the HVAF-i7 process.

proposals.material_system: FeCoNiCrAl HEA powder (15–45 μm) using HVAF-i7 deposition
proposals.intervention: Adopt a dual-pass (layer-by-layer) deposition strategy with in-situ reheating between passes
proposals.conditions: HVAF-i7 deposition performed in sequential passes on substrates with constrained geometries (internal diameters ~120 mm), with controlled in-situ reheating of the freshly deposited coating to a moderate temperature (e.g., 150–200 °C) between passes
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced interlayer bonding and reduced thermal mismatch
proposals.mechanism: Depositing the coating in multiple thin layers enables each pass to consolidate and bond well to the substrate and the previous layer. In-situ reheating reduces thermal gradients and residual stresses while promoting diffusion-assisted bonding, allowing for a thicker composite coating without compromising adhesion or oxidation resistance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: An overall thicker, multi-layered bond coat with high integrity and minimal oxidation, surpassing the thickness limitation of a single-pass deposition, yet retaining performance under high-temperature service.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This strategy targets the thickness issue by breaking the deposition into controlled subsections, ensuring each layer deposits optimally while cumulatively achieving the desired thickness.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly leverages evidence from conventional MCrAlY studies that indicate higher particle velocity improves deposition efficiency. By tuning the propellant gas mixture (via adjusting the fuel-to-oxygen ratio), the HVAF-i7 process can impart higher kinetic energy to the FeCoNiCrAl HEA particles, thereby enhancing splat formation and reducing the likelihood of particle rebound. This mechanism directly targets the inadequate thickness issue observed with the standard process, and the approach remains applicable in geometrically constrained applications (e.g., internal diameters as small as 120 mm). Although other approaches (such as substrate pre-heating or dual-pass deposition) have potential merits, they either do not as directly address the thickness limitation or introduce additional complications. Therefore, we adopt direction D.
